Alice.summary: Misleading statements and lies are equally wrong because both involve the intention to make the listener believe a falsehood.

Bob.summary: Misleading statements are always wrong, but lies are not always wrong, and lies do not necessarily require an intention to deceive.

c1.text: A lie is a statement made with the intention of making the listener believe a falsehood as if it were true.

c2.text: A misleading statement is a statement that is true but easily misunderstood by the listener.

c3.text: A lie can be made even without the intention to deceive the other person.

c4.text: A brazen insistence that one is innocent when everyone knows the truth is a lie told without the intention to deceive.

c5.text: Both lies and misleading statements can involve the intention to make the listener believe a falsehood.

c6.text: Misleading statements and lies are equally wrong.

c7.text: Misleading statements are always wrong, but lies are not always wrong.

c8.text: Scientists whose sincere predictions later turn out to be false are not morally blameworthy.

c9.text: There can be statements that are true but still morally blameworthy.

c10.text: Misleading statements and lies differ in their degree of moral wrongness.

a.note: Alice agrees that lying requires deceptive intent (c1); Bob disagrees by arguing that a lie can occur without deceptive intent (c3).

b.note: Both agree that misleading statements are true (c2) and can be morally blameworthy (c6 for Alice, c7 for Bob), deriving c9.

c.note: Alice explicitly argues that lies and misleading statements are equally wrong (c6, contrary to c10), so she does not hold c10.
